Let me preface: I love this game and this trilogy. I despise EA. I also wanted to play this on my Steam Deck to relive those glory days of incredible multi-player with my friends. Sadly, the game barely functions with a controller, even with the most highly rated controller setting in the game's library. 

In other words: This is the most amazingly nostalgic 60fps game I have seen on the Deck that cannot be played properly, and thus you will not be able to enjoy it.

Oh, and the EA App is ridiculous, and it took me half an hour just to get through those hoops after over seven different authenticator codes and loops to jump through with my own data, just to play the game and find out it doesn't even work properly. Oh, and while I connected my Xbox account to my steam account, I still had to start completely over with no data.
Clunky, Ugly, Unwieldy, I got it as a gift and to be honest was miserable the entire time I was playing it.

The multiplayer still works, and still kicks ass, tested 25/06/25.

Mods allow you more to do than the Legendary Edition, but it's hard work and slowly becoming harder as tech moves on.

Only buy for MP, go for the Legendary Edition if that doesn't interest you

Mass Effect 3 N7 Digital Deluxe Edition (2012) delivers the explosive conclusion to Commander Shepard’s original journey, combining cinematic science-fiction storytelling with squad-based role-playing and faster third-person combat. Developed by BioWare and published by Electronic Arts, it begins with the Reapers launching their devastating assault on Earth and other major civilizations across the galaxy. Shepard is forced to leave humanity’s homeworld and return to the Normandy, beginning a desperate campaign to unite species that have spent generations divided by political disputes, warfare, prejudice, and historical grievances.

The story succeeds largely because it treats the Reaper invasion as both a galactic catastrophe and a personal crisis. Shepard encounters returning friends, former squad members, political leaders, soldiers, and civilians whose circumstances may reflect decisions carried over from earlier games. Long-running conflicts involving major species finally reach decisive moments, and several story arcs receive emotionally powerful conclusions. Loyalty, sacrifice, diplomacy, and survival constantly intersect, giving many decisions more weight than a simple choice between obvious good and bad outcomes. Players who import a character from previous installments receive the strongest sense of continuity, although newcomers can still understand the central conflict.

Gameplay is noticeably more responsive than in the earlier entries. Shepard can move between cover positions more smoothly, perform evasive rolls, execute heavy melee attacks, and engage enemies at a quicker pace. Firearms feel effective across the various weapon categories, while biotic and technological abilities remain essential components of combat. The class system allows players to specialize in direct gunplay, devastating biotics, engineering abilities, stealth, or hybrid approaches. Power combinations are particularly rewarding, since properly coordinating Shepard’s abilities with those of squad members can trigger powerful effects against groups or heavily protected targets.

Squad selection remains strategically meaningful. Companions possess different strengths against armor, shields, barriers, synthetic enemies, and ordinary infantry, encouraging experimentation with team composition. Character progression and equipment customization provide flexibility without burying the player beneath unnecessary complexity. The balance leans more heavily toward action than the first Mass Effect, but enough RPG mechanics remain to make character builds, dialogue decisions, relationships, and squad development important throughout the campaign.

The galactic war structure gives most major missions a clear purpose. Shepard must gather fleets, personnel, technology, intelligence, and other military resources before confronting the Reapers. This makes diplomatic missions especially important because resolving an old conflict can influence the strength of the coalition. The game is at its best when military necessity clashes with personal loyalty or historical resentment. Decisions can require Shepard to consider immediate survival against consequences that may affect entire civilizations, reinforcing the idea that commanding the resistance involves far more than simply winning firefights.

This Digital Deluxe release is particularly appealing because of its extensive additional content. From Ashes introduces material connected to the Protheans and adds valuable context to the universe. Leviathan explores mysteries surrounding the origins of the Reapers and provides some memorable atmospheric sequences. Omega offers a more combat-oriented storyline centered on reclaiming the famous space station, while Citadel provides a more relaxed and character-focused experience that celebrates Shepard’s relationships with the crew. The Extended Cut also expands the ending with additional scenes and explanations, giving the finale more context than the original launch version.

Multiplayer content further broadens the package through cooperative battles in which teams fight waves of increasingly dangerous enemies while completing objectives. Different playable species and classes provide considerable variety, especially when players coordinate powers to create combinations or cover weaknesses within the team. Additional multiplayer expansions increase the selection of characters, maps, equipment, and enemy encounters. Various weapon, armor, appearance, and equipment packs are also included, making this edition a substantially more complete version of the 2012 release.

Presentation remains impressive for a game from its era. War-torn cities, alien environments, futuristic installations, enormous spacecraft, and familiar locations create a convincing sense that the entire galaxy has become a battlefield. Strong voice acting gives the returning cast personality and emotional credibility, while the soundtrack effectively moves between desperation, quiet reflection, military urgency, and large-scale cinematic spectacle. The Normandy continues to function as an important emotional center where conversations between missions provide welcome relief from the constant pressure of the war.

The experience is not without shortcomings. The greater emphasis on shooting means players looking for the slower exploration and heavier RPG structure of the first game may find the design more streamlined than expected. Some secondary assignments are less memorable than the major narrative missions, and the ending remains potentially divisive even with the Extended Cut improvements. The requirement for an EA account and additional EA software can also make launching the Steam version less convenient than a completely self-contained Steam release.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unsupported. Players primarily interested in experiencing it on Valve's handheld should keep this limitation in mind rather than assuming that the simple controls automatically guarantee full compatibility. Its design may appear ideal for portable play, but the official Deck classification does not currently provide that assurance.

Despite those drawbacks, Mass Effect 3 N7 Digital Deluxe Edition remains a remarkably ambitious finale. Its strongest moments come from seeing relationships, rivalries, political conflicts, and decisions accumulated across the trilogy finally collide with the Reaper war. Excellent characters, satisfying combat, meaningful choices, substantial DLC, cooperative multiplayer, and an appropriately enormous sense of scale make it an impressive conclusion, particularly for players already invested in Shepard and the Normandy crew.

Rating: 9/10
